title: Painting Scope Gaps: Surface Prep, Primer Coats, and Spec Requirements GCs Underspecify
summary: Missed primer coats and vague surface prep language cost GCs on every painting package. See which Division 09 requirements get overlooked at bid.
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


- Painting scope gaps rarely come from missing line items — they come from vague surface prep language and unspecified coat counts.
- Division 09 specs are where the money hides. "Paint as per specs" is not a scope of work.
- The most expensive gaps are substrate-specific: drywall, concrete, ferrous metal, and galvanized steel all need different prep and primer systems.
- Subs exploit ambiguity at buyout. GCs who front-load specificity win the margin game.
- Provision's[Scope Agent](https://provision.com/scope-agent) reads the full project set — drawings, specs, and addenda — to surface these gaps before bid day.


Painting looks simple on a budget. A number goes in the painting line. The sub prices it. Everyone moves on.


Then buyout happens. The sub's scope excludes primer on CMU. Or the spec calls for three coats on high-humidity areas and the sub bid two. Or surface prep for ferrous metal isn't mentioned anywhere — not in the scope sheet, not in the sub's exclusions.


Those gaps don't disappear. They show up as change orders on a job that was supposed to be clean.


This article breaks down exactly where painting scope gaps form — from Division 09 spec requirements to surface prep language to coat count disputes — and what GCs can do to close them before bid day.


## Why Painting Scope Gaps Are Underestimated


Painting feels like a low-risk trade. Unit costs are familiar. Most estimators have a gut feel for what a typical floor costs to paint.


That familiarity creates complacency. And complacency is where scope gaps live.


The[Scope Gap Playbook's trade-specific chapter](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook/trade-specific-scope-gaps) documents how gaps cluster in trades that feel "solved." Painting is a textbook example. The line item is always in the estimate. The detail behind it often isn't.


Three conditions produce painting scope gaps more than anything else:


1. **Vague scope language** — "paint all walls per specs" tells no one anything actionable.
2. **Substrate diversity** — one project can include drywall, CMU, concrete, wood, ferrous metal, and galvanized steel. Each needs a different system.
3. **Spec complexity** — Division 09 painting sections can run 20–40 pages. No one reads all of them on a tight bid schedule.


As one Pre-Construction Lead at a Top-ENR Canadian GC put it: *"If you miss anything, they'll bill it."*


## The Most Common Painting Scope Gaps by Category


### 1. Surface Preparation Requirements


Surface prep is where most painting disputes start. It's also the most underspecified line item on a typical GC scope sheet.


Division 09 painting specs almost always define prep requirements by substrate. But scope sheets rarely carry that detail forward. Instead, they say something like "provide all labour and material for painting as per specification."


That language sounds complete. It isn't. Subs will interpret it in their favour.


The specific prep requirements that get missed most often include:


- **CMU block filling:** Spec may require block filler as a separate product applied before primer. Subs often price primer directly to bare CMU without a fill coat — which the spec explicitly prohibits.
- **Concrete surface profile (CSP):** High-performance coatings on concrete slabs or walls often require mechanical prep to achieve a minimum CSP. That's labour cost the sub may not have included.
- **Ferrous metal:** Surface prep standard for ferrous metal is typically SSPC-SP6 or SP10. Wire brush and one coat isn't the same as a near-white blast. The spec defines which standard applies.
- **Galvanized steel:** Galvanized surfaces need chemical prep or a specific adhesion primer. Subs who miss this line in the spec will apply standard primer — and it won't bond.
- **Drywall:** MPI or manufacturer specs often require skim coat or Level 5 finish before painting in high-gloss or semi-gloss applications. If the drywall sub's scope doesn't include Level 5, and the painting sub's scope assumes it's done, no one does it.


That last scenario is a coordination gap. It doesn't live in one trade's scope — it falls between two. Those are the hardest to catch without reading the full project set together.


### 2. Coat Count and System Specification


Division 09 specs define paint systems — not just colours. A typical spec will designate a system number (e.g., System 9B) for each substrate and describe the primer, intermediate coat, and finish coat required.


Most sub bids price two coats on drywall and call it a day. If the spec calls for three coats in high-traffic corridors or high-humidity spaces like kitchens, locker rooms, or mechanical rooms, that's real money left unpriced.


The gaps that cost GCs most often:


- **High-humidity rooms:** Epoxy or semi-gloss systems in mechanical and wet areas often carry a three-coat requirement. A sub pricing standard latex will miss this entirely.
- **High-traffic wall systems:** Some specs require a high-build intermediate coat in corridors or stairwells. That's an extra pass most subs won't include unless it's explicitly called out in the scope.
- **Fire-rated assemblies:** Intumescent paint on structural steel is sometimes spec'd under Division 09. If it's not in the painting scope and not in the steel scope, it belongs to no one.
- **Existing surfaces on renovation work:** Reno specs routinely require additional coats over existing painted surfaces to achieve coverage. Subs pricing new-construction coat counts on a reno job will underrun.


### 3. Millwork, Doors, and Frames


Painted millwork and hollow metal doors and frames create a classic coordination gap — one that mirrors the gypcrete naming collision documented in[the Scope Gap Playbook's trade chapter](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook/trade-specific-scope-gaps) .


The painting sub assumes hollow metal frames come factory-primed and only prices finish coats. The hollow metal sub prices supply-only with shop primer. No one prices field touch-up and finish coats. The GC gets a change order request on day one of painting.


The same pattern applies to:


- Wood doors — factory-primed or not, field-painted or not, how many coats
- Exposed structure — if beams, columns, or deck are exposed and painted, who scopes it
- Mechanical and electrical equipment — whether painting of equipment rooms, pipe chases, or exposed ductwork is included


### 4. Scope Boundaries: What's "Paint" and What Isn't


Division 09 painting specs typically define the scope of work for the section. But the edges are blurry — and that's where GCs lose money.


Common boundary disputes include:


- **Exterior vs. interior painting:** If the spec has separate sections for exterior and interior systems, make sure both are in the scope sheet. A sub quoting "interior painting" on a building with painted exterior CMU panels won't price the exterior.
- **Roof screening:** Painted parapet walls, screening panels, or mechanical curbs at the roof level are sometimes in Division 09, sometimes in Division 07. If neither scope sheet names it, neither sub includes it.
- **Traffic markings:** Parking garage line painting, stencils, and curb marking are often in a separate spec section (09 96 00 or similar). They're routinely left out of the painting scope sheet and don't show up elsewhere.
- **Firestopping colour coding:** Some jurisdictions and specs require colour-coded firestop sealants or painted identification on penetrations. That's not painting scope — but if the GC doesn't explicitly assign it, no one prices it.


## The "As Per Specs" Problem


The single most common anti-pattern in painting scope sheets is the phrase "as per plans and specs."


It sounds comprehensive. It protects nothing.


When a dispute happens, the sub's position is simple: "We priced our standard system. If you wanted something different, you should have specified it." The GC has no ground to stand on because the scope sheet never defined what "something different" looked like.


The Scope Gap Playbook's anti-patterns chapter names "as per plans and specs" as the most-cited failure across 200+ GC interviews. The problem isn't that it's technically wrong — it's that it transfers all interpretive risk to the sub, and subs interpret ambiguity in their favour.


One Estimating Manager at a Canadian ICI GC put it plainly: *"We have less subs who just kind of a gentleman's agreement… they've become more quick to clarify that we're not including that one piece of scope."*


The fix isn't longer scope sheets. It's specific scope sheets. Define the substrate. Name the system. State the coat count. Cite the spec section.


## How to Write a Tight Painting Scope of Work


Good painting scopes share four traits. They name the substrate. They cite the system. They define the coat count. And they call out exclusions explicitly so there's no room for "we assumed."


Here's what that looks like in practice:


Weak Language Strong Language


Paint all walls per spec Apply System 9B (primer + 2 finish coats, eggshell latex) to all GWB wall surfaces per Section 09 91 23


Paint CMU as required Apply block filler + primer + 2 finish coats to all interior CMU surfaces per Section 09 91 23, System 5C


Ferrous metal painting included Prep all ferrous metal to SSPC-SP6, apply epoxy primer + alkyd finish per Section 09 91 13


Touch-up as required Touch-up of hollow metal frames (shop-primed by others) — 2 finish coats, field-applied, per Door Schedule note 3


Exterior painting included Exterior CMU painting excluded — refer to Section 09 96 53 (elastomeric coating, bid separately)


The right-column language takes longer to write. It takes far less time than the change order that comes from the left-column version.


For a baseline document structure, Provision's[scope of work template](https://provision.com/resources/scope-of-work-template) gives estimators a starting framework — but the spec-specific detail still needs to be read and applied by trade.


## What Division 09 Specs Actually Require (and What Gets Missed)


Division 09 painting specifications are organized by MasterFormat. The sections that generate the most scope gaps are:


- **09 91 13** — Exterior Painting. Often split from interior, often missed in scope sheets that only reference "09 91 23."
- **09 91 23** — Interior Painting. The core section. Contains substrate-specific system tables. Most subs price from system column one — read all the columns.
- **09 96 00** — High-Performance Coatings. Epoxy, urethane, and elastomeric systems. These carry higher prep requirements and coat counts. Frequently confused with or folded into standard painting scope.
- **09 96 53** — Elastomeric Coatings. Exterior CMU and concrete wall systems. Often a separate bid package — but if it's not explicitly excluded from the general painting scope, subs and GCs argue over who owns it.
- **09 72 00** — Wall Coverings. Not painting — but proximity in Division 09 means it sometimes gets lumped in. Define it separately.


Addenda are another risk point. If the architect issues an addenda that changes the paint system from System 9B to System 9D on a specific substrate, a sub who didn't read the addenda prices the wrong system. The[Chat Agent](https://provision.com/chat-agent) can pull addenda changes against spec sections in under 20 seconds — which matters when you're 48 hours from bid day and have six addenda to reconcile.


## Buyout: Where Painting Gaps Become Disputes


Scope gaps don't always surface during bidding. Many survive all the way to buyout — when the awarded sub presents exclusions that weren't in their original number.


The pattern is predictable. A sub submits a bid that says "painting per plans and specs." The GC awards on that basis. At buyout, the sub's scope sheet excludes block filler, excludes primer on galvanized steel, and excludes high-performance coatings in mechanical rooms.


Each of those items has a cost. Together, they can add 10–20% to the painting package.


The Scope Gap Playbook's third habit — *front-load the buyout conversations* — applies directly here. Before award, get the sub to confirm the coat system, the prep standard, and the specific exclusions in writing. A five-minute conversation at pre-award is worth more than a two-week change order dispute at substantial completion.


The[Risk Review](https://provision.com/risk-review) tool surfaces contract language that creates risk before you sign. On projects where "readily inferable" scope language appears in the prime contract, knowing which painting items fall under that clause matters — because the GC may absorb costs the sub won't carry.

## Summary: The Painting Scope Gaps Worth Closing First


Not all scope gaps carry the same dollar risk. For painting, the highest-priority items to lock down on every bid:


1. **Surface prep by substrate** — define the prep standard for each substrate type in the project. Don't assume.
2. **Coat count by system and location** — reference the spec system table. Corridors, wet areas, and mechanical rooms often carry different requirements than standard spaces.
3. **Block filler on CMU** — this is the single most commonly missed prep item in painting scopes. Name it explicitly.
4. **Galvanized and ferrous metal systems** — confirm prep standard and primer type are in the scope, not just "paint included."
5. **Hollow metal doors and frames** — clarify whether shop primer counts as the first coat, who does field touch-up, and how many field coats are required.
6. **High-performance coatings** — confirm whether 09 96 00 and 09 96 53 sections are in or out of the painting scope. If in, define the system and prep requirement separately.
7. **Addenda changes to paint systems** — check every addenda for system changes before closing the sub's scope.


The firms that win margin on painting aren't doing anything exotic. They're reading the spec, carrying the detail into the scope sheet, and having the buyout conversation before award. That's it.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### What are the most common painting scope gaps on commercial construction projects?


The most common gaps are surface prep by substrate (especially CMU block filler and ferrous metal prep standards), coat count discrepancies in high-humidity or high-traffic spaces, missed high-performance coatings in mechanical rooms, and ambiguous scope boundaries between interior and exterior painting sections. Most originate in Division 09 spec language that never gets carried into the scope sheet.


### What does "as per plans and specs" mean in a painting scope of work?


"As per plans and specs" sounds comprehensive but protects the GC from almost nothing. It transfers all interpretive risk to the sub, who will price their standard system. When the spec requires something beyond standard — more coats, a different prep standard, a high-performance product — the GC has no documented basis to hold the sub to it. Name the system, coat count, and spec section explicitly.


### How do Division 09 painting specs create scope gaps?


Division 09 painting specs define paint systems by substrate and location — not just colour. System tables specify primer type, coat count, and finish for each condition. Scope sheets that don't carry this detail forward leave subs free to price their standard system. Gaps form when the spec requires a higher-performance or multi-coat system and the scope sheet says nothing more than "paint per spec."


### Who is responsible for painting hollow metal doors and frames?


This depends on what the spec and scope sheets say — and that's the problem. Hollow metal subs typically supply frames with shop primer. Painting subs often assume shop primer counts as their first coat, or that they're only pricing finish coats. If neither scope sheet defines field coats and touch-up explicitly, the GC ends up holding the gap. Resolve this at scope issuance, not at buyout.


### What is the difference between standard painting and high-performance coatings in Division 09?


Standard painting (Section 09 91 23) covers interior latex and alkyd systems on typical substrates. High-performance coatings (Section 09 96 00) cover epoxy, urethane, and elastomeric systems used in mechanical rooms, wet areas, and exterior CMU. They carry higher prep requirements, different application standards, and higher material costs. Painting subs pricing standard systems won't include high-performance coatings unless the scope explicitly assigns them.


### How can GCs prevent painting change orders during construction?


Write scope sheets that name the substrate, cite the spec system, define the coat count, and state exclusions explicitly. Front-load the buyout conversation — confirm the sub's system and prep standard before award, not after. Read addenda for system changes before closing the scope. And treat "as per plans and specs" as a red flag, not a complete scope description.
